title: Understanding Your Average Salary Melbourne: Hourly to Annual with Casual Loading and Super
description: Convert your hourly rate to annual pay using the average salary Melbourne as a benchmark. Includes casual loading, super, tax, and fortnightly breakdowns.
salarySummary: For a casual worker earning $33.05 per hour (including 25% loading) working 38 hours per week, the annual gross pay is approximately $65,300 before tax and super.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my annual salary calculation?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an additional 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave. When converting to annual pay, you multiply the loaded rate by hours per week and 52. For example, the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour becomes $33.05 with loading. If you work 38 hours per week, your annual gross is $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,300.88. Super is then paid on top of this amount at 12%.

faqs.q: What is the average salary Melbourne and how does it compare to my hourly rate?
faqs.a: The average salary Melbourne is not a single figure but varies by industry and occupation. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports national full-time adult average weekly earnings of $2,083.70 (May 2026), which is about $108,352 annually. For Melbourne, state-level data may differ. Use the [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page to find industry-specific averages. Your hourly rate multiplied by 38 hours and 52 weeks gives an annual figure you can compare against these benchmarks.

faqs.q: Is superannuation included in my hourly rate or paid on top?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings, not included in your hourly rate. The super guarantee is 12% of your gross pay (up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830). For example, if your annual gross is $65,300, your employer must contribute an additional $7,836 into your super fund. This is separate from your take-home pay and is not subject to income tax until withdrawn.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay

If you earn an hourly wage or are considering a salary offer, understanding how to convert that figure into an annual amount is essential for budgeting and comparing job opportunities. The standard formula is simple: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. This gives your gross annual pay before tax, super, and other deductions.

For most full-time roles, the typical working week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. When we say “full-time” in this article, we assume 38 hours per week unless stated otherwise. If you work part-time or different hours, adjust the weekly hours accordingly.

### Including Casual Loading

If you are a casual employee, your hourly rate usually includes a 25% casual loading. This loading compensates for not receiving paid sick leave or annual leave. The [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains how it works. When calculating your annual pay, use the loaded rate. For example, the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour for permanent employees. With casual loading, it becomes $33.05 per hour. Multiply that by 38 hours and 52 weeks: $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,300.88 per year.

Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading into the [timesheet](/). The timesheet has a checkbox to add 25% loading on top of your base rate. Always enter your base hourly rate (without loading) and tick the box if you are casual.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many Australians are paid fortnightly. To find your gross fortnightly pay, simply multiply your weekly pay by 2. Using the casual example above: weekly pay = $33.05 × 38 = $1,255.90. Fortnightly = $1,255.90 × 2 = $2,511.80. This can help you match your budget to your pay cycle.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top

Your employer must pay superannuation guarantee contributions on top of your ordinary earnings. The rate is 12% of your gross pay, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. Super is not deducted from your hourly rate; it is an additional cost to your employer. For the casual example, annual super would be $65,300.88 × 12% = $7,836.11, paid into your nominated super fund. This is separate from your take-home pay and is taxed at 15% when it enters the fund.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Your annual gross pay is subject to income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income between $18,201 and $45,000
- 30% on income between $45,001 and $135,000
- 37% on income between $135,001 and $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (based on 2025–26 single reduction thresholds as 2026–27 thresholds are not yet confirmed). For a gross annual income of $65,300.88, the tax would be approximately $9,267 (using the 2026–27 brackets) plus Medicare of $1,306, leaving an estimated take-home pay of $54,727. Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page for a more detailed estimate.

### Comparing to the Average Salary Melbourne

When evaluating your pay, it helps to compare against benchmarks. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reports that national full-time adult average weekly ordinary time earnings were $2,083.70 in May 2026. That equates to an annual salary of about $108,352. However, this is a national average across all industries and states. The **average salary Melbourne** may differ due to local industry mix and cost of living. For example, Melbourne’s average might be higher in professional services but lower in hospitality. To find industry-specific or state-level averages, refer to the [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page which draws on ABS data and Fair Work classifications.

It is important to note that these averages are not medians. The average can be skewed by high earners. Your own pay should be compared to award rates or market rates for your specific job. The [job pay](/topics/job-pay) page provides guidance on finding award classifications.

### Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour (from 1 July 2026). This applies to employees not covered by an award or enterprise agreement. Many industries have award rates that are higher. For example, the Hospitality Award may have different rates for different levels. Always check the relevant award via the Fair Work Ombudsman’s [pay guides](/blog) or the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page. Casual employees receive the 25% loading on top of the award rate.

### Summary of the Formula

Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52.

For a permanent full-time employee on the minimum wage: $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,245.44.
For a casual on the minimum wage with loading: $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,300.88.
Super is 12% on top: $7,836.11 for the casual example.

Use the [reference tables](/data) to see common conversions. Remember that this calculation assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. It is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.
